title: Playing school houses in Alabama and staying with teachers
summary: They played schoolhouses for percentage of gate, with crowds of hundreds, and stayed in teachers' homes.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Must have drew some ladies to those clubs.

So we used to work every night and the weekend in Alabama, didn't have no nights on. Every night and the weekend. We'd play school houses, no night club, we'd play school houses and have them just stand up against the wall in auditorium. Very few clubs, we'd play about, we'd go out on a ten night or fifteen night thing, we'd probably play about three clubs about the whole fifteen nights, the school house. We had to set up from one school to the other. And see that each month they would call us back, each hour we'd come back, and when the first school called them we'd just notify the other school we'd come back and every one of them booked us. Because if they weren't guaranteed, they'd only give us a percentage of the dough, they'd took twenty and give us eighty. But you see, and believe it or not, at that time, some schools were only charging a dollar, some would go a dollar and ten cents. Yeah, well they'd have five to six hundred school kids, plus other people from the streets, you know, who'd come to their dad. So enough when you have a seven, six, seven, eight hundred

dollar dough. In course eight hundred dollars. And most of those places would people come, I don't know, would people, I know maybe in the small ones, would people come to dance to what Slim was doing? Right, right. They'd come to see the heaven in auditorium. They'd be dancing, they'd be dancing. But they would dance.

Oh yeah, and drinking their moonshine or liquor, whatever. Yeah, they'd come out there. And most every school house we would play, they'd be packed. And we'd play every school, believe it or not, at that particular time, you couldn't stay, black couldn't stay in a hotel, because they hadn't passed that bill. So we'd stay at different teachers' houses, you know. See, we notified the school we were coming. And they said, you have to make a range for us to stay. We've got eight to nine, ten pieces, whatever. And so what the principal would do, he'd see this lady, and the different neighborhood, you know, can you keep two, can you keep one? And they wouldn't charge you for the dollar pieces there all night, you know. They're in their own neighborhood. So we even got to buy cheaper. And some of them used to fix the food for us.
